items.title: [Read-along] The Odyssey, W.H.D. Rouse, Books I - III
items.text:
*Below I am starting the book club, as promised previously. It has probably taken longer than I originally led on. I expect that this can be forgiven. Whether you took up the challenge or not, there may be something for you in the following post. I have made an effort to give some original thoughts, followed by a character list and book summaries. As mentioned before, I am reading a hard copy of the translation of W.H.D. Rouse, but I can also recommend the* [*digitized version of the translation of A.S. Kline.*](https://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odhome.php)

***

# leading themes and ideas

* post-war society leads to excess and decay
* culture, values, family, country -- all need to be defended by their inheritors
* the most commonly held belief is not always the correct one

# Commentary

The first three books show how Telemachos has been living and responding to the apparent death of his father, Odysseus. Unbeknownst to Telemachos, his father is lost at sea, dealing with cyclops, and upsetting Poseidon in the meantime. With the help of other greek heroes (Achilles, Agememnon, Nestor, Menelaus etc.), Odysseus led the Achaeans to victory at the battle of Troy, and since then, things have not been going so well back home. This is the setup for the poem.

This is a story of what happens in the aftermath of war, when a great society produces heroes that defend its culture and norms against outsiders, and how, despite their victory on the battlefield, this same culture must be defended in their absence. This is seen at the outset, when the gods discuss what has become of the house of Atreus, whose son, Agememnon, finds himself the victim of Agisthos. The latter is eventually murdered by Agememnon's own son, Orestes, in an act of revenge for the murder of his father and the destruction of his household. Zeus laments the fact that, although they have brought this terrible fate upon themselves, men continue to hold Zeus to account. Wherever the fault lay, the poem tries to reckon with the phenomenon where society grows weak in the absence of the warriors who will defend their culture.

As the drama of the poem ensues, it is revealed how political infighting led the Achaeans to split up after Troy, leaving Agememnon and Odysseus away from their homeland. In the latter's absence, his wife Penelope and his son Telemachos have been left to defend what is left of his household. Suitors consume Odysseus' wealth, as they loiter, courting Penelope.

**So far, I have taken the following from the poem, summarized in a few sentences:**

* A great culture, such as the Greeks had, will produce great warriors, in whose absence its greatness will quickly fall to shambles.
* There will always be those willing to feast on the spoils bought by the sweat and blood of another person's brow
* Even when an entire population believe one thing, it may not be true. Truth is not easily discerned, but found out through persistence, struggle and adventure.

So, to you, reader of Epic poetry, I ask the question:

* Where do you see yourself on this cycle (i.e. good times --> weak men --> bad times --> strong men?)
* Is there an analogue in modern culture to the suitors feasting on Odysseus' wealth?

***

# Reading notes:

key characters

* Odysseys: a great warrior from Ithica. Never returned from the battle of Troy, in which he earned his stripes as a hero.
* Telemachos: the son of Odysseus.
* Penelope: the wife of Odysseus. Awaiting Odysseus' return.
* Suitors: men gathered in Ithica, enjoyers of Odysseus' house and belongings, as they vie for Penelope's hand in marriage.
* Zeus: Father of the gods. Feels let down by mortal men because of what happened in the aftermath of the battle of Troy concerning Agememnon.
* Aigisthos: killed Agememnon and married his wife. Is then killed by the latter's son, Orestes.
* Agememnon: in the aftermath of the battle of Troy, did not wish to sail home, for fear of displeasing Athena. He splits from Diomedes and Nestor, and stays in Troy
* Athena: Zeus' daughter. Favors Odysseus, intervenes for him so as not to see his house come into ruin
* Poseidon: god of the seas
* Mentes/Mentor: Athena in the form of a man, advises Telemachos in Ithica and in Pylos.
* Aigyptios: Wise councilman, blesses Telemachos
* Nestor: son of Neleus, king of Pylos.

# Book Summaries:

## Book I

> These men amuse themselves with music and song, freely, since they consume another’s wealth without repayment, one whose white bones are tumbling in the waves, or rotting in the rain on some far shore
> \--Mentes.

Zeus and Athena meet on Olympus. Lament Agememnon's murder and betrayal by Aigisthos. Athena descends from Olympus to intervene into the affairs of Telemachos, to keep him from a similar fate. His father, Odysseus, suffers the ire of Poseidon, who keeps him from returning home against the will of the other gods. Suitors, who think Odysseus is dead, harass Penelope and Telemachos, and take advantage of the latter's good manners. No one really knows whether Odysseus has died. Telemachos answers Mentes that he does not stop the suitors from courting his mother for the dread of not knowing what has come of his father. Before transforming into a bird to depart, Athena rouses Telemachos to gather the lords together and order them to stop, and moreover, that he should go out in search of his father.

## Book II

> ‘My lords, my Suitors, though Odysseus is dead and you are eager for me to marry, have patience till I complete this work, I do not want it wasted, this shroud for noble Laertes, ready for when pitiless death’s cruel end overtakes him: since I fear some Achaean woman of this land would blame me, if he who won great wealth lay there without a shroud.’
> \--Penelope

Telemachos assembles the lords of Ithica and makes his case, demanding that and end be put to the suitors' behavior. Antinous rebukes him, saying that Penelope has tricked them for the past three years, by saying she would choose a husband when the finishes weaving the shroud of Odysseus' father, Laertes, which she would work on during the day only to unravel the work she had completed under the darkness of night. Zeus sends an omen portending the destruction of the suitors. Athena again urges Telemachos to go in search of his father, provisions a ship and a crew for him, and even afflicts the suitors in Telemachos' home with drowsiness. Telemachos sets sail for Pylos in search of news of his father.

## Book III

Telemachos arrives at Pylos, where the people all pay sacrifice to the gods. Telemachos and Mentor make an offering to Poseidon, in Nestor's name. Telemachos appeals to Nestor, who also fought at Troy, to give news of what happened to Odysseus. He reports that the latter was caught in the middle of a feud between Menelaus, who wished to depart after the battle of Troy, and Agememnon, who feared the angering the gods, and wished to wait. Nestor and Odysseus went with Menelaus, leaving Agememnon behind. In a moment of hesitation, however, Odysseus turned back to join Agememnon. Nestor and Menelaus sail from Troy together and in the meantime, Aigisthos overtakes Agememnon, killing him and taking his wife for marriage. Nestor urges Telemachos to look on the heroism of Orestes, who took revenge against and murdered his father's murderer, Aigisthos. He tells Telemachos he needs to visit Menelaus for news of what came of Odysseus. Nestor offers Telemachos his men and ships, his hospitality, they sacrifice a heifer to Athena, and set off at dawn.

items.title: Swing and a miss: Paying with Bitcoin on a Square Terminal
items.text:
This year, I've got my kids doing a homeschool co-op two days a week. This just means that a group of homeschool parents have organized to teach their children in a group setting, and possibly hire a teacher or two for subjects where more formal education might be helpful (languages, music, science?). 

Unfortunately, the coop we have joined is quite some way from our home, so after dropping off the children, I go to a nearby coffee shop to work -- a coffee shop that has a Square terminal.

I have asked if they accept Bitcoin a number of times so far, but in all cases the cashier's answer has been "I don't think so" or "I'll have to talk to the person who manages this" (pointing at the terminal). It's a busy place and so there is often a line, and I haven't wanted to try to make anyone wait while I help figure out how to turn on Bitcoin payments, and so I haven't made much progress. 

Today, the person behind the cash register was the owner and I seized my opportunity. 

I placed my order and while he was ringing it up, I said, "I've heard that these Square terminals accept bitcoin."

The owner glanced up at me and said, "I've heard that, too. Let's see if we can figure it out."

This was a much more enthusiastic response than I was expecting. He poked away at the terminal for a few minutes and then said, "I think it only takes bitcoin if you have CashApp."

I told him that this was not the case, but that if he could get it to display a QR code I could try paying that.

He continued to tap on the terminal without much effect. I should say this terminal was not the sort that has a rotatable screen. There is one fixed screen facing the cashier and a smaller fixed screen facing the customer. This was showing the message "Waiting for cashier..."

"I think you have to tap to pay," he said.

Now, I don't use any of the Lightning wallets that have implemented tap to pay (as far as I remember there aren't very many) so that wasn't an option. I told him that I needed a QR code to scan.

After another couple minutes, the owner volunteered: "Maybe I can text it to you." 

I am usually loathe to provide a phone number, but in the interest of dismantling the legacy financial system, I gave it to him. I immediately received a text with a link. The link was to pay for my coffee, but had required fields for name, phone number, and email. At the bottom I saw a green button that said pay with CashApp or something like that. I tapped it, but nothing happened because I had not entered the required fields. 

Still in the interest of taking down the fiat empire, I entered some incorrect information in these fields. But then when I tapped the green button, it presented me with a message informing me that I did not have CashApp and a button to download CashApp. 

At this point the line behind me was long enough that I offered to pay with cash and the owner accept with some visible signs of relief.

So: I have failed on this the fourth time I've tried to pay with Bitcoin at this Square terminal. I suspect that the owner needs to turn Bitcoin payments on and that I will need to talk him through this process, so I'll have to rewatch those videos about how to do this. 

It occurs to me that Square could do a lot better with this flow if they had a button that allowed the cashier to display a QR code that was simultaneously a CashApp code and a Lightning invoice. This is a lot to ask, but I'm pretty sure it needs to be at least that easy for it to work well.

items.title: How to Get People to Use Bitcoin
items.text:
For many years, I’ve been trying to figure out how to get bitcoin into people’s hands. Even long-time bitcoiners often don’t want to pay with bitcoin. At best, they slowly accumulate it, and they don’t really feel like they’re missing anything. They buy it on exchanges, pay fees, expose their personal information, and need a third party’s blessing for every transaction.

I sometimes hear people say that bitcoin doesn’t need anyone and that, on the contrary, we need bitcoin. I see it a little differently. To me, bitcoin is something like a living organism. I consider its creation to be an event almost as rare as the emergence of life itself. But for bitcoin to truly live and serve us as better money, I believe it needs users.

With every transaction, a new connection is created or an existing one is strengthened. Users gradually get better at securing their bitcoin, demand better tools, and bitcoin becomes more resilient.

That’s why I don’t think adoption is some kind of optional bonus.
**Adoption is a fundamental condition for bitcoin to actually be useful.**

## I tried various approaches

* I liked the idea of bringing bitcoin directly into Signal, for example: https://stacker.news/items/85702
  * But Signal still hasn’t added bitcoin support, and I’m afraid there simply isn’t enough incentive for them to do so anytime soon.
* Years ago, I also created an app that allowed people to load bitcoin onto an NFC card and pass it around much like cash: https://stacker.news/items/117623
  * Technically, it worked. But there wasn’t enough interest. It was a nice project, but it didn’t solve a real problem for people.
* Later, I also looked into why even bitcoiners themselves often don’t want to pay with bitcoin: https://stacker.news/items/210830

## It’s not enough to let merchants accept bitcoin

In the meantime, I onboarded dozens of businesses and bitcoiners locally.

Most of them were just isolated points on a map. A business started accepting bitcoin, but nobody actually paid with it. Eventually, the merchant forgot how to accept a bitcoin payment or what to do with the bitcoin they received.

It wasn’t until about a year ago that I managed to partially break through this problem.

I onboarded another business simply because we went there regularly. And to this day, every week we come there in a changing group of people, with everyone paying in bitcoin. https://stacker.news/items/1584550

![](https://m.stacker.news/159586)

The pub owner didn’t want bitcoin at all in the beginning. What matters to him is us as customers who come to his pub because of bitcoin. In the end, a merchant will accept pretty much any form of payment. What’s more important is finding people who are willing to pay with bitcoin.

Here, we use bitcoin also as a filter for finding interesting people. Anyone willing to pay with bitcoin is kind of open-minded, and it’s a pleasure to get to know them over a regular lunch.

## I don’t want to depend on a single app again

Over the years, I’ve recommended various wallets and tools to people. Some of them eventually disappeared.

The custodial version of Wallet of Satoshi, which was the most popular one, stopped working. Alza, the largest retailer in the Czech Republic and one of the first major merchants to accept bitcoin, started requiring additional administrative steps when paying with bitcoin. Qerko, which allowed bitcoin payments at around 1,000 businesses, removed bitcoin support.

At first, this was pretty discouraging. It was the end of 2025, and at the same time the price of bitcoin dropped significantly. I had to figure out what to do with the dozens of people I had introduced to a particular app, which was now no longer going to work for them.

I felt a little trapped. With every app, there was a risk that I would have to repeat the whole migration process again at any time.

But in January 2026, it also seemed to me that AI models had improved significantly, so I decided to try building my own wallet. One that I had been carrying around in my head for years.

## Linky

Linky is a bitcoin wallet and, at the same time, a communication layer for the people you want to use bitcoin with.

You can add your contacts, send them messages and bitcoin. You can pay any Lightning invoice. You can load bitcoin in the form of Cashu tokens onto an NFC card or send it to someone in a message — even to someone who doesn’t use Linky at all.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159587)

But I’m also trying to build a certain degree of antifragility into it.

From the beginning, I’ve been building Linky so that the app doesn’t depend on a particular operator. There are already other instances running on different domains. If my instance stopped working tomorrow, the network wouldn’t necessarily have to disappear with it.

We achieve this through a combination of three decentralized technologies:

* **Cashu** for bitcoin,
* **Nostr** for communication,
* **Evolu** for data storage.

We use several other interesting technologies as well, but I don’t want to get into the technical details here. There are now six other developers working on Linky. One of them is a close friend of mine who has been improving the app very intensively, primarily on the technical side.

What started as a funny vibecoded app is gradually becoming a serious project.

Around 250 people are currently testing Linky in the local group, and several hundred more users are using it.

## Individuals

People use Linky because they like it.

Thanks to its simplicity and steadily increasing reliability, it is gradually becoming the primary bitcoin wallet for many people.

**However, most people still don’t actually need a lightning wallet.** 😢

You can build a great wallet. You can onboard merchants. You can explain the benefits of bitcoin to people.
But if they have no reason to use bitcoin, all of those things will remain just flashes of activity.

## Proxy Payments

Recently, however, we managed to create a feature that I think can at least partially solve this problem. We call it **proxy payments**.

In the Czech Republic, people increasingly use QR codes for bank transfers. You can find them in online shops as well as physical stores.

For users, this is still somewhat less convenient than paying by card, but merchants love it because they don’t have to pay card-network fees.

Today, I can pay with bitcoin at any of these businesses. No fees and no KYC.

I scan the payment QR code using Linky - just as if I were paying a lightning invoice. Linky offers me the option to send the payment request to my contacts.

I select several friends and send them the offer.

Whoever accepts it first receives the payment details from the QR code. They pay the merchant from their bank account, and I send them sats in return.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159589)

## Does it worth the effort?

Maybe this sounds like a pointless detour. Why would I ask someone else to pay by bank transfer on my behalf when I could simply pay myself?

For me, it’s useful because I don’t have to hold fiat that is losing value.

For my friends, it’s useful because they don’t have to use an exchange, pay fees, or expose their personal information. They acquire bitcoin in an interactive way — usually in small amounts.

As a side benefit for everyone, there is the more abstract fact that you are building the bitcoin network and thereby helping ensure that you’ll be able to use bitcoin in the future as well.

To use proxy payments comfortably, you need roughly two or three people. Most payments are completed within two minutes. It’s not as direct or fast as paying by card, but it works surprisingly well.

Linky is showing people new ways to use bitcoin.

**Come help us test and build our shared bitcoin network. 🙏**

items.title: Bank Runs are Good, Actually: Death to the Central Banks (FT, Toby Nangle)
items.text:
ASTONISHING piece to see in regular financial press. *Maybe the tide is turning and the world is healing?*

![](https://m.stacker.news/159395)

The basic/most fundamental rationale for a central bank isn't financing the gov deficit (which they don't...*ish*) or set centralized interest rates, but to support commercial banks when faced with bank runs (=stand ready to lend against their assets, even if distressed, with newly created base money, so stave off the run.) The idea, from Francis Barings to Diamond\&Dybvig's [Nobel Prize](https://stacker.news/items/1583458?commentId=1583534) winning article, is that depositors are fickle and might/will run on perfectly healthy banks *and* that such runs cause real damage to the economy (*and* might spread through the banking system like wildfire and we all collapse into Great Depression 2.0).
*That's everything that's wrong with monetary economics and politics around central banks in one sentence...*

***

The authors of the paper Nangle discusses here used the Chronicling America project, scanned newspapers, then...

> they used LLMs to sift these articles further to find pieces about actual bank runs rather than, say, stuff about boats running into river banks, or the local bank manager running for mayor, and to match each report to individual banks.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159396)

> According to Verner, the research reveals that the idea that runs kill solvent banks is dramatically overstated. It turns out that depositors are actually pretty good at working out how dodgy a bank is, generally making runs on banks that are insolvent or very close to insolvent.

This is incredible. Specifically, — and I'm sparing you a deep dive into debates in financial history and monetary economics here — a big rationale for *why central banks must exist* is **to prevent bad types of bank runs.**

Running a bank means it has to shed assets, assets that aren't "finished," or turned into workable projects and thus liqudity, yet. (That's sort of the purpuse of a bank: to *liquify* illiquid assets, hold the maturity and duration mismatch in the meantime.)  Selling these assets quickly means taking (large) haircuts on book value, meaning a random run on a healthy bank can destroy projects or at least turn the bank itself bankrupt -- destroying customer relatioships and disrupting the bank-money-level money supply etc etc. 
**That's all unnecessary, and a benevolent central bank/observer can improve upon the state of the world by injecting more money and support the healthy bank.**

## ...except, depositors don't run on healthy banks!

That's what this beautiful history and database shows. Somehow, depositors (in aggregate) are clever enough to sniff out when something is wrong *and not* structurally/mindlessly/sunspot-style make erratic and concentrated mistakes.

If you scratch [the lender or last resort literature a little](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/when-did-the-bank-of-england-become-a-lender-of-last-resort/), you find that it's a good, disciplining market mechanism for depositors to run on banks. Here's a schematic:

* if bank is healthy and other bankers know it, then the bank can source enough liquidity from them ("recycling" deposits), against a very minimal short-term expense. **No problem, no negative outcome, no need for lender of last resort** 
* if the bank is unhealthy and the other bankers know it, they won't lend to it and it will fail, *and it will be a good thing!* Bankers taking bad risks or making bad investments should fail, like every other business in a market economy.
* if the bank is healthy, but the **other bankers don't know it** *and so refuse to lend*, that's when a lender of last resort needs to step in and save the day. By supplying that extra liquidity it can stave off the damaging run and everyone is better off for it.

Here's the best short article/overview I've ever seen on this (by [George Kaufman, for econlib](https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/BankRuns.html)):

![](https://m.stacker.news/159394)

---

The literature on bank runs and central banks is basically an exercise in showing **whether or not the central bank knows about the true state of a given bank better than other bankers do.**

When central banks *also* had prudential obligation, by chance some of its workers would have recently audited and inspected private information for that bank, meaning it's quite plausible that central bankers *do* have some insider information here that they can act on. (Nowadays that function is usually separated to another agency, thus the argument is practically quite moot.)

But... If historically and practically depositors are good enough in aggregate to sniff out what's wrong, there's no *need* for a central bank to intervene and override their market choice.

Bank runs are bad for local economies

> ...only if the banks that are being abandoned have been making bad loans, a big borrower defaults, or something like that.

...in which case there is **a real economic loss that we want/need someone to carry** — not paper over and pretend it's not there. (\_cough\_, Bitfinex...)

***

Told yah:

> Surely **the mere process of a run on a healthy bank wreaked havoc on their local economy?** Apparently not.

> Cross-referencing each bank’s financial strength, the researchers trace the local economic impact of each bank run using Bradstreet’s contemporary reporting. They find that a run on a strong bank doesn’t really impose any economic cost at all on the local economy. Yet runs on banks whose fundamentals are awful are followed by major lending contractions that can cause all sorts of spillover problems.

and:

> Out of **3,984 bank runs on individual US banks from 1863–1934**, the authors identify 53 that look like they’re based on “misinformation” or “depositor confusion”, which reads as academese for “blind panic”. Of these 53 oddities, six banks failed, which sounds like maybe six too many. But the researchers argue that the historical data indicates that “strong banks (fundamentals in the upper tercile) subject to **non-fundamental runs have a zero probability of failure”**
> one of the footnotes indicates that at least one of these failed banks had basically committed massive fraud, which was only uncovered by their so-called irrational run.

*Even that*, the depositors sniffed out. Amazing.

***

All "pretty interesting" says Nangle, understating the explosive result.

> the ideas that the Nobel winners formalise are really the ones sitting behind the rationale for bank deposit insurance.

Yes. This evidence shows/weighs heavy that lender of last resort is a defunct and unnecessary function — liable to abuse, nepotism, and trigger-happy rulers, not actually saving a banking system that needs it

## Runs are good. Banks should fail more. And lender of last resort is an unnecessary function

items.title: How life gets in the way of Stacker News
items.text:
I’ve been largely offline and not really on SN much these days. Mostly a collection of small things, like health issues that aren’t in the “oh shit” realm, but which take up lots of time and energy (neither my wife nor I have figured out how to stop getting older - other than the one obvious one - and that means more health bullshit each day, apparently). Plus work just being, well, work. And assorted miscellaneous things. Much as I love SN, I only have so much time in a given day.

But this in turn has made it clear how much I need a better subscription page for SN. When I do have time for SN, I hit my subscription page and it’s fucking overwhelming. If I’m lucky, I can see maybe twelve hours worth of stuff, but sometimes, it’s only a few hours.

I subscribe to maybe eight territories, and maybe as many individual posters. But that’s enough (especially as some of the territories have gotten busier) to completely overwhelm my feed. I’ve missed plenty of important posts ([one costing me 10K sats](https://stacker.news/items/1571441) [^1]), and plenty more where I’d have loved to contributed to discussions.

One obvious solution would be to just reduce what I subscribe to. But that’s self-defeating. I subscribe to people and communities because I like them and want updates. I also (obviously) want notifications on posts I make and when I’m tagged.

What I’d like (and I have no idea if this is on the radar, nor if it’s easy/possible) is the ability to break up my subscription page. The aggregate page is fine when I’m on a lot. But when I’m not, allow me to see territory subscriptions from separately from the user subscriptions separately from the comments on my actual posts. I could manually just change all my settings each time, but if I had the time to do all that all the time, I’d have the time to keep up with my feeds. As it stands, having a lack of time to keep up with SN is, in itself, something that causes me to fall behind even further on SN.

I'm always reluctant to request features/changes that may only help me, but putting this out there as something that others who are short on time (assuming I'm not the only person whose entire life doesn't revolve around SN) might also want to weigh in on?

[^1]: Not really, since I’d have lost eventually, and probably soon. But I can keep telling myself that's not true.

items.title: Book Review: Broken Money and the Way Out, PART 1: MONEY (the Invity Team)
items.text:
TAKEAWAY NUMERO UNO: If there's a successful book titled *Broken Money*, you DO NOT title your own marketing pamphlet/e-book style "Broken Money" as well.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159635)

***

I spent some time today looking through the Invity people's fintech offering. We met at BTCHEL, where they launched/announced some cool banking features for us Europooreans. https://stacker.news/items/1580878, https://stacker.news/items/1581849 https://stacker.news/items/1585380

Particularly, quite convenient **auto-stacking, payment cards with bitcoin/stablecoins,** and **juicy-af cashback** on every spend. (Up to stupidly [low maximums](https://www.invity.io/personal-accounts), it turns out -.-)

This is all very tempting, and Den is a sucker for a good sats deal (*aren't we all?!*), so what does a bookish nerd do?

## Download and read the free e-book, of course!

***

It's from their educational platform, Invity Academy (as if we didn't have enough educational outlets...):

> It is meant for people who know Bitcoin from headlines and debates, but never got an answer to the most important question: why did it come about at all, and what problem does it solve?
> We start with money itself — how it came about, how it works today, and why so many people feel that something about it „broke“. Only once we understand the problem does it make sense to talk about a solution.

Oh, turns out this is *really* for Mr. Den. Let's dig in.

*Blah-blah-blah*, money's three functions, and various properties (ignoring, for now, Erik Yakes' *7th Property*, **Immutability** https://stacker.news/items/1572208)

![](https://m.stacker.news/159636)

...gold, commodity money, stock-to-flows. Alright, amazing. State intervention, Roman coins.

## "If you were born after 1971, you live in a historical anomaly"

Pretty neat account:

* 1870-1914: Classical gold standard
* 1933: gold banned
* 1971 Nixon Shock

They definitely overdo the importance of 1971, a mere formality in a world already addicted to fiat and money printing. (1914 is a more important civilizational cutoff.)

Cool, but graphs like these are pretty boring. A *dollar*, like *a* bitcoin, is not a meaningful economic unit; nobody (rationally) cares about *a* dollar, but the relationship between what they have and earn to what they invest and consume. e.g., https://stacker.news/items/737272, https://stacker.news/items/1578595

![](https://m.stacker.news/159637)

> 1913 the Fed, 1933 the ban on holding gold, 1944 Bretton Woods, 1971 the Nixon Shock — four steps from hard money to fiat. → Since 1971 no currency in the world has been backed by anything tangible

VERY nice

![](https://m.stacker.news/159638)

> How money is actually created today
> → The vast majority of the money in your account was created by commercial banks, not the state.
> → New money comes into being at the moment of a loan. When you repay the loan, the money disappears.
> → QE lets a central bank create money in the order of trillions within weeks.
> → The M2 money supply grows substantially faster than real output.

## AMAZINGLY witty: "Money-supply inflation is the cause, price inflation is the symptom."

![](https://m.stacker.news/159639)

Here's a scary graph, but of course *financing conditions* matters too: An average interest rate for mortgages in Czechia was about [7% in 2000](https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Average-mortgage-loan-interest-rate-1995-2005_fig7_24080862); [below 5%](https://www.globalpropertyguide.com/europe/czech-republic/mortgage-interest-rate) in 2025.

## Inflation as a silent tax

![](https://m.stacker.news/159641)

> Modern central banking is often defended with the argument that it stimulates the economy and creates jobs. Even if we take that at face value, we must at the same time see the flip side: the money a central bank creates does not arrive for everyone at once. It travels a predictable path that structurally favours one group over another.

VERY eloquent and punchy.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159640)

> At the end of the pipe stand

* **The fixed-wage employee**: the wage is usually adjusted only with a delay, and not by the full extent of inflation.
* **The pensioner** — the pension is indexed once a year, slowly.
* **The young family** without assets — they own no assets to rise in value, yet pay higher prices for food, energy, rent.
  -**The saver** on a savings account — the interest does not cover the loss of purchasing power

These things are conditional and not *obviously* and *always* the case; boomers in America enjoy pretty competitive COLAs; interest rates on savings accounts in Iceland are ~halfway between CPI and monetary expansion. With bond prices collapsing, rates on (high-yield, short-term) bank accounts like those at fintechs are bound to rise explosively. https://stacker.news/items/1578425

***

## NOTHING STOPS THIS LYN ALDEN TRAIN

Yeah, dudes didn't just *borrow* Lyn's title; they take her fiscal framework too: there's no way back/out from governments' profligacy and debt-to-GDP ratios. America just *cannot* outgrow [40trn in debt](https://stacker.news/items/1554591) (...unless we scalp the boomers https://stacker.news/items/1468968, you know the drill.)

> An economic term returning to the debate in recent years is fiscal dominance. It means a state of affairs where the state’s budgetary situation is so strained that the central bank cannot run an independent policy. Lyn Alden describes that the United States entered this situation around 2022. The interest cost on US federal debt exceeded the defence budget in 2024 — and that is a defence budget which is itself larger than the budgets of the next ten largest countries combined.

The financial FIXES that used to work:

* The **60/40 portfolio**: yeah, it's entirely dead. Also, bonds don't provide *neither* uncorrelated returns, nor inflation-adjusted returns at all.
* savings account: guaranteed losses. Czech republic example is \~4% interest on savings, 2.5% official inflation... BUT tax the nominal return 15% *and* assets like flats and properties rose *way more* than 1-2%.
* New fixes?

> Holding large cash in the bank is, over the long run, a strategy by which the state really taxes your purchasing power. Diversification remains valuable, but it must include assets that respond to monetary degradation (hard assets). Gold passed the test of 5,000 years. Neutral, apolitical, independent of the banking system. Bitcoin is new — it has 15 years behind it. But if its properties are confirmed, it offers everything gold does, and more: portability, verifiability, divisibility and neutrality in a form gold can never have.

...in PART 2, dudes move on to the orange solution: \_bitcoin\_, woop woop!

items.title: My dearest Chloe and her in-home euthanization
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/157540)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157477)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157491)

These were the earliest pictures of Chloe I had available to me. We got her when she was 9 years old while living in Hawaii where she was born and raised. A navy family was moving and had three cats but when it came time to move to a new location the navy would only pay to move 2 and they had to select a cat to stay. Against their hearts wishes, they chose Chloe. They chose her to stay because they knew just how special she was and how loving and adaptable she would be in a new home. Chloe was a homie through and through. She wanted to explore and chill with a human companion. So in mid 2016 we took her home and fell in love.

![](https://m.stacker.news/157480)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157551)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157493)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157554)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157555)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157492)

These were in the second place we moved with her on Island from 2017-2019. She was so beautiful outside. We'd let her roam around as she pleased and she was good to come back even when you called her! (sometimes a little persistence was needed). She'd bring us critters, proud as ever, and once she brought me a little finch. I was making dinner at the time and in she comes with what I thought was a dead bird but when she put it down it flew away in hasty evasion! So the bird is flying around the house, Chloe is re-chasing the bird, and I am chasing Chloe.

![](https://m.stacker.news/157543)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157550)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157546)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157542)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157474)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157553)

These were taken throughout the years 2020-2025. At this point we had moved off island to California where she continued to roam and walk outside. She loved that fireplace every winter! We also noticed early on that she loved to rest her head on things so we gave that little pillow you see on the chair to her. She loved that pillow. If she was laying anywhere without it, we'd go get it for her and put it next to her and she'd use it right away. She'd also loved a good arm. She would jump up on the couch or come to you on the floor and wait for you to put your snuggle arm out so she could curl up inside.

![](https://m.stacker.news/157476)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157549)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157556)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157552)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157548)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157544)

![](https://m.stacker.news/157541)

As her little joints began to weaken, we had to give her those stairs there so she could get down from the couch without jumping. She was very thankful. These pictures are from 2025 to the end of her 19.5 year long life in early 2026. She developed a tumor on the side of her head, and it eventually started to interfere with her motor system. She was the best animal. A true companion. Her ability to sense emotion was uncanny. If someone was sad or my wife was having a bit of an overwhelmed angry episode, Chloe would come. She was a mediator and always a calming presence and it seemed like she took on that role with intention. I miss her dearly and I am extremely thankful to have had the fortune of having such a companion.

I wanted to share also her journey of euthanization. I was surprised to find out that in-home euthanization was a possibility and I'm sure there's some variance to the service as a stranger needs to come to your house but really, I couldn't recommend it enough. Chloe was achy and confused and the last thing I wanted to do to her was bag her up and bring her to a foreign place to die. There are many options for this, if you look. The lady that came over was so caring and loving and understanding and did an excellent job making sure everyone involved had whatever they needed.

items.title: Another day, another project 🌅
items.text:
Hello frens!

How have you been? I hope you're doing good and are healthy wherever you might be. 

They say idle hands are the devil’s playground, and I have so many projects waiting for me but, like most people, not nearly enough time. But that’s another conversation.

Anyway, I kept myself busy last week and this week too with a project I’ve been coming back to for quite a while. I’m so happy I finally made the time to make it real!

When I stumbled upon this project, I was very excited about it, [Using NeoPixels with the Raspberry Pi.](https://thepihut.com/blogs/raspberry-pi-tutorials/using-neopixels-with-the-raspberry-pi) I thought, “Maybe instead I could make a sunrise lamp.”

And boy, was it a journey.

Even before I started researching, I thought the best Raspberry Pi for such a simple project would be a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. Unfortunately, I couldn’t find one, so I decided to go with the next best option especially since I was already brainstorming what else I could do with it besides the sunrise lamp. So I got a Raspberry Pi 3 B+.

Let me walk you through it.

First, it was a bit of a nightmare to install the OS. I don’t know why I struggle with that part and with passwords. I type passwords the way R. L. Stine writes his stories: with just one finger. Either way, I finally managed to install everything and connect to the Wi-Fi.

I knew I would eventually need an electrolytic capacitor and one of those logic level shifters, but for the first trials—just trying to get the Pi and the LEDs working—I left those for later.

I also need a proper power supply for the LEDs themselves. I’m still not entirely sure, since it’s only 32 LEDs, but we’ll see. The preventive side of me will probably end up getting one anyway.

I had to test the first LED strip, but first I had to connect everything to the right GPIO pins and solder the wires. Usually my husband helps me with this part, but he only helped me with the first strip. After that, I was all on my own.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/be570358-1cbc-4a6b-8bc3-ac87d29ad61a_img_8973-213.04.16.gif)

I didn’t know soldering would be as challenging as stripping the wires, but once I got the hang of it, things went much more smoothly.

I did a lot of the research and troubleshooting myself, and for the scripts I also tried a bit of vibe coding. But hey, I was still the one soldering, wiring everything up, testing it, and figuring out what was going wrong. Then I ran the test and… it worked!

But then, of course, came the real challenge... soldering everything together! All the wires and the LED strips.

I had to use the headlamp I use when walking my doggie, and next time I’ll definitely need a magnifying glass. I had to squint from time to time just to make sure I was soldering in the right place.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/55cf9895-d39e-4dc7-9f9f-ad913e468d69_img_9007.jpeg)

I managed to do the devil’s work, I mean, my project, and then I used another script. But before that, I had to install Python in a virtual environment, because otherwise it wouldn’t let me install rpi\_ws281x.

It seems this way is easier to update and keep contained, and it doesn’t affect the rest of the Pi. Also, this time I did everything directly in the terminal. I didn’t use Thonny this time!

So many firsts with this project.

Anyway, in the end, my soldering and the script worked together beautifully!

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/b1a2dfb4-0a23-43af-bf60-3d60bdca4f3d_img_9051.jpeg)

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/24206c44-4240-4671-9556-44dbe83451bd_img_9052.jpeg)

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/e3e233b0-ab4b-4f07-aca9-3ba325358b80_img_9053.jpeg)A sunset right there just for me!

Throughout all this testing, I kept sniffing the Pi and the GPIO area from time to time, just in case I had connected something wrong. After all, powering the LEDs directly from the Pi could be too much for it.

Slowly but surely, I was able to turn the LEDs on and off first. Then I added the sunrise and sunset scripts.

After that, I moved on to the web server. Since I had already dipped my toes into this with [my Raspberrarium](https://stacker.news/items/1541799), I decided this time it wouldn’t just show me information, it would also have buttons to control the LEDs.

Then I added a “reading mode,” a “fun mode,” and a “relax mode.”

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/ea3f6f09-d876-468c-a8ba-16ca6c9813bc_img_9003.jpeg)

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/d82ea84c-1bd2-49b2-99d8-d7cec3dfdd37_img_9017.jpeg)Reading mode

I got super excited watching the first sunset that day. Every five minutes, I would just look at the LEDs slowly dimming.

This week, I added a few more buttons to the web server: some colors, dimming controls, and “demos” of the sunrise and sunset scripts.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/8572001d-7983-45fe-ba49-cedaa6a376a0_img_9054.jpeg)Sunset and Sunrise have buttons though they are running automatically in the background. I still kept them because it reminds me of how this project started. 

What a ride it was!

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/e04c6ebc-0ddc-41f8-885e-c3e097a648a1_freecompress-img_9019.gif)Rainbow mode

And I’m not finished yet. This is still a work in progress, and I’ll add a few more things. I’m so happy with it.

I feel like a wizard.

So, see you later, alligator!

items.title: You Can See Everything - Review
items.text:
## **You Can See Everything**

⚡️⚡️⚡️⚡️ 4/5 Zaps. Worth the sats to see in theaters. One of the best things of the year!

***

https://youtu.be/GGJSRFWALTI?si=7qSyHQI45xohKwnN

I’ll start with what worked, move to what didn’t, and then wrap with the ending and final thoughts.

**TLDR: “You Can See Everything,” is rightly titled because afterward your left wondering what ‘exactly’ did you see.**

***

I don’t think I can rightly review this without **spoiling** everything so starting now consider everything after this with **spoilers**, also should mention you should go into this **unspoiled** if you plan on watching it. I don't think you should watch it any other way. Lastly I have stayed away from every trailer for this movie on purpose, minus this [first teaser.](https://youtu.be/GGJSRFWALTI?si=JYfn_LyZYjCfRSsu)

***

## The Setup

![](https://m.stacker.news/161736)

I don't think this is a documentary in the traditional sense. There's something really interesting about the way the filmmakers carefully control what the viewer gets to see, often presenting events through a collage of tightly framed portrait shots, deliberately staged moments, and sequences that don't necessarily unfold in chronological order.

In fact, I'd be interested in watching this a second time for that reason alone. I suspect knowing what I know now would make it easier to distinguish what's authentic, what's staged, and what's been deliberately manipulated to shape our understanding of the story.

I'm also deliberately calling it a *"thing"* throughout this review because I genuinely don't know what else to call it. It's not exactly a traditional documentary, but it's not entirely a movie either. Much of the second half feels almost entirely like a feature film, with moments that seem so bizarre and unrealistic that you start wondering how much of what you're watching is actually happening the way it's being presented.

And I keep coming back to this point because somewhere around the halfway mark, you realize you're no longer just watching a documentary. You're on a [*"journey"*](https://youtu.be/_8AYmVyIFsc?si=upY9YeUt1HA-2K2E) with Nathan.

But then you begin to realize something else, Nathan isn't necessarily showing you events in the order they happened, nor is he giving you the complete picture. He's carefully deciding what you get to see, when you get to see it, and how you're supposed to interpret it.

That's when I started questioning Nathan himself as a reliable storyteller of what we’re watching because he might be getting tizz whispered by Elizabeth Holmes for most of this.

***

## The Good

![](https://m.stacker.news/161739)

Having said all that, I think what they're doing is brilliant. They're attempting something very few documentary filmmakers have dared to do, openly challenge the idea that you can trust the filmmaker to give you an accurate account of what you're seeing. I know it sounds funny to make this comparison, but there's almost a Christopher Nolan philosophy at work here. Nolan's filmmaking is predicated on trusting the intelligence of his audience, allowing viewers to question what they're seeing and piece things together for themselves.

The filmmakers behind *You Can See Everything* seem to operate from that same philosophy. They don't assume the audience is dumb or incapable of recognizing the sleight of hand happening right in front of them. Instead, they invite you to notice it and purposefully lean into at times that doesn't feel entirely on the nose. I wouldn't call the manipulation necessarily a flaw in the documentary, I think it might actually be the entire point.

The film does this fascinating thing where you think you're watching one story unfold, only to realize Nathan has been showing you exactly what he wants you to see at that particular moment. Then, just when you think you've figured it out, your understanding of what you've been watching completely changes.

I know this might sound like I'm flustered or confused by the whole thing, but I'm really not. Quite the opposite, actually. I think this particular story needed that kind of manipulation of events and perspective to make the whole thing work. And I have to say, this was probably the fastest three hours I've ever spent watching anything.

As for the story itself, it takes you on a wild ride that constantly has you questioning everything you're watching. It starts with Elizabeth Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, but eventually that same skepticism extends to Nathan himself. Nobody is really off limits, including the guy making the documentary.

One of the most interesting surprises, though, is the introduction of [Amanda Seyfried](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1086543/), who, at least for me, ends up stealing the entire movie in what initially seems like a supporting role.

She first enters the documentary to reenact scenes the *You Can See Everything* filmmakers weren't there to capture, including moments from before filming began and later events while Elizabeth Holmes is in prison. But then something really interesting happens. Amanda stops being just an actress recreating events and becomes an actual character in the documentary itself, largely because of Billy Evans' seemingly insatiable need to confront her personally.

Amanda was incredible in [The Dropout](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W7rlZLw9m10), so seeing her show up here genuinely caught me off guard. I'm so glad nobody spoiled that for me. My immediate reaction was basically, [*hmmm, what is she doing here?*](https://plebtv.com/v/the-californians-edit-36cd6601d6) lol.

But what starts as a somewhat bizarre casting decision eventually becomes one of the film's most important elements. Amanda ends up serving as something of a reliable witness within this increasingly unreliable documentary, even calling Nathan out on some of his own bullcrap toward the end.

Just when you've gotten comfortable questioning Elizabeth Holmes, Billy Evans, and their version of events, the documentary turns that same scrutiny back on Nathan.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161737)

Something stackers might enjoy, one interesting thing, is they do bring up cRyPto twitter, and they're is a prominent account that you do see for a split second. You do later find out that Billy her husband is tweeting on her behalf. 🫠

Speaking of money, **greed** is undeniably one of the central themes of this whole thing. You could almost argue that an alternative title for *You Can See Everything* could've simply been *Greed*.

Towards the latter half of the documentary, greed practically steals the show. It becomes this underlying force driving just about everyone involved: A24, Nathan, Elizabeth Holmes, and her husband Billy. Everyone has something to gain, something to protect, or something to lose. And I think that's precisely why this whole thing is so brilliant. It feels entirely intentional, like the YCSE filmmakers are deliberately pulling back the curtain on the very incentives driving the people making and participating in the documentary itself.

And when you combine that greed with the strange dynamics of Elizabeth vs. Amanda and Nathan vs. Billy, the whole thing becomes this bizarre, almost recursive, meta exercise. It's turtles all the way down, except every turtle has its own agenda, its own version of the truth, and its own financial incentives.

***

## The Bad

![](https://m.stacker.news/161738)

There's honestly not a whole lot of bad I can say about this movie, but there are a few things worth mentioning.

For starters, I think watching it with an audience was somewhat enjoyable in the beginning. There's something fun about experiencing a movie this strange with a room full of people who are just as confused or surprised as you are. But as the film went on, some of the things people were laughing at weren't particularly funny to me, and that eventually became a little annoying.

Things also get pretty heated when Amanda starts arguing with Billy, especially when some of her [past comments](https://x.com/DiscussingFilm/status/1998889970942226937) come back into the conversation, particularly those surrounding Charlie Kirk. This is where the theater experience really started to take away from the movie for me. People in the audience began doing that thing where they talk back to the screen, shouting some genuinely awful things that I really wish I hadn't had to sit there and listen to.

And for the record, I saw this movie in Georgia after TabConf, not Texas.

There's also an early nude scene that I thought was pretty dumb and completely unnecessary. It felt like it was thrown in for no other reason than to get a cheap laugh. In a thing that's otherwise so deliberate about what it chooses to show you and why, that moment felt especially out of place.

***

## Final Thoughts

![](https://m.stacker.news/161740)

I'll just end by saying that *You Can See Everything* is genuinely one of the most meta things I've ever watched in my life. It's the kind of film that makes you question not just the story being told, but the very nature of storytelling itself, especially when the people telling the story have their own incentives and agendas.

I genuinely think Nathan and his team might be stumbling onto, or perhaps deliberately inventing, an entirely new genre of documentary filmmaking. It blurs the lines between documentary, performance, manipulation, and reality in a way that feels uniquely suited to his style.

It's rare to watch something that makes you question so much while somehow keeping you entertained the entire time, and leaves you wondering if everything is just a mindgame. Looking forward to see what they create next.

***

items.title: You Walk Your 10k Before Lunch, Anon? (The Economist)
items.text:
**Ah yes, that 10k step goal:** I'm doing ok on the new regime... 9,746 seven-day average!

> Conventional wisdom sets 10,000 steps per day as a good target. The source of that number, though, is as questionable as Hippocrates’s quotation. Its origins lie not in a clinical trial, but a Japanese advertising campaign for a pedometer launched ahead of the 1964 Tokyo Olympics (10,000, in Japanese Kanji, also looks a little like a person walking). Those committed to getting their steps in should not shy away from the 10,000 mark. But in terms of scientific research, the number barely has a leg to stand on.

You *kind of* need a lot of imagination to make this (万) look like a guy walking. [https://www.kanshudo.com/kanji/%E4%B8%87](https://www.kanshudo.com/kanji/%E4%B8%87)

> A study published in *Lancet Public Health* in 2025 considered 57 papers published since 2014 to assess the connection between different daily step counts and various health outcomes. Walking more was found to be beneficial across the board. Taking 7,000 steps a day, in contrast to 2,000, brought about a 47% lower risk of premature death, a 25% lower chance of developing cardiovascular disease and a 14% reduction in the risk of diabetes. Even a little goes a long way: going from 2,000 daily steps to 4,000 resulted in a 36% drop in mortality risk over the years tracked.

wow, *extraordinary!*

## "Extra steps keep helping, but beyond around 7,000 per day, they are scarcely worth the effort. The jump from 7,000 daily steps to 10,000, for example, led to only a 2% further reduction in mortality risk."

> Any reasonable amount of walking is better than none. But for those unable to walk much, upping the pace might be a way to increase the benefits.

...and how neat:

> “And if you don’t have enough opportunities,” says Dr Stamatakis, “create them.” Rather than parking right outside the supermarket, for example, stop around the block and do a walking sprint in.

Bitcoin-related context from the report:

## The US is importing digital gold and exporting digital dollars

Congressional passage of the GENIUS act in mid-2025 formalized what crypto economies around the world already know: the U.S. is the leading exporter of digital dollars. Stablecoins have turned US debt into a currency-of-choice for peer-to-peer economies as well as businesses working across borders. In the 2026 period we continued to see stablecoins enter new use cases most especially abroad, benefitting the U.S. companies, and the U.S. government, with billions of dollars in economic activity.

While the U.S. has been exporting stablecoins, it has also been importing bitcoin. Since the January 2024 launch of the spot bitcoin ETFs, the U.S. share of global bitcoin activity has consistently risen through every reporting period. Meanwhile, stablecoins make up a smaller share of American crypto activity than of activity elsewhere, and the gap has widened each period Indeed, the chart below shows this trend. It pools three measures (Bitcoin’s share of service inflows, of exchange trading and of net cross-border receipts) into a single index, so the distance between the lines, not their height, is the finding. The divergence shows the growing US dominance in Bitcoin and the rest of the world becoming increasingly dependent on USD stablecoins.

[![](https://www.chainalysis.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/bitcoin-and-stablecoin-intensity-united-states-against-the-rest-of-the-world-1500x804.png)](https://www.chainalysis.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/bitcoin-and-stablecoin-intensity-united-states-against-the-rest-of-the-world-scaled.png)

A dollar stablecoin is a way to hold dollars without an American bank account, and Americans already have one. The rest of the world is pivoting to a digital dollar because it meets a need that American users don’t share. Meanwhile, Americans are leaning harder on bitcoin as an infinitely scarce store of value. “Investor interest in bitcoin as a monetary alternative remains strong, particularly as government debt and spending reach new highs globally,” says Will Su, Managing Director and Head of Digital Assets Research at BlackRock.

Counting all cross-border bitcoin flows into and out of the US, the country became a net importer in 2026 for the first time since 2022. Transfers under $10,000 ran net outbound every period measured. But larger denomination transfers flip to net inflows, with the bracket above $10 million alone accounting for 53,200 coins arriving. Retail sends bitcoin out; institutions bring it in. A federal Strategic Bitcoin Reserve has added implicit sovereign demand to the private bid, even without an explicit buying program.

items.title: This one hits the nail on the head, about the manufactured homelessness crisis
items.text:
This article really resonated with me. I formerly lived in a city where homelessness went from a minor issue to a festering sore that couldn't not be ignored, and caused everybody to avoid the downtown.

And then it spread like a cancer, via the building of enabling "no barrier homeless shelters" in the suburbs, that made the whole AREA, not just the downtown, into a urine-soaked and crime-ridden unlivable space.

People who don't live in places like this don't know how bad it can get. I assure you, it can get very bad, and doesn't take that long. Public spaces can easily be absolutely destroyed by a small number of people who are allowed to do whatever they want (defecate, be loudly vocally crazy, camp in tents, etc.) in those public spaces.

Here's the article: 

[https://naomiwolf.substack.com/p/the-homelessness-industry-oregon](https://naomiwolf.substack.com/p/the-homelessness-industry-oregon) 

It should be available without a login.

A few quotes:

> By the latest visit, as I knew would be the case, almost no one who was not homeless or drug-addicted, could enjoy the beautiful square. A few children did still play in the enclosed playground, guardians or parents watching them warily.
> But no one strolled the walkways. No one lounged on the grass. Young women in groups, or as singles, wearing bikini tops and shorts, or crop tops, no longer lay on beach blankets to sun themselves, or to listen to music on their headphones. Couples did not lie together any longer gazing into one another’s eyes. Young men did not play Frisbee. Middle schoolers did not ride their scooters around the walkways or gather to gossip and laugh in groups. Elders did not sit on the benches. Moms did not bring their babies to lounge on the lawn and play.

> No one picnicked. Have you noticed the quiet death of the picnic?

> All of these things used to happen, in public spaces like this one in America. Not so long ago. I remember them.

***

> We talk about the loneliness of the elderly. But now they can’t meet their old friends or make new friends, in what had been a safe “third good place.”

> We worry about kids on screens all day, becoming depressed and anxious, sedentary, risking obesity and related illnesses. But older kids and teenagers can’t go to this little park any more by themselves, to socialize and get fresh air and exercise.

> We worry about the destruction of community. But this policy around homelessness literally destroyed a space that created and nurtured community.

> Is this situation artificially created and sustained, for ulterior motives?

(The answer to the above is YES, absolutely. Very on-the-nose article, and if you haven't lived in an area where  homelessness has become a real problem, read it to understand more).

items.title: BlitzPerp: Inverse Perpetual Futures on Statecoins
items.text:
On most exchanges, your position is only a row in the exchange’s database. BlitzPerp keeps it on Bitcoin. Each side of a position locks its margin in a statecoin, a Bitcoin output whose ownership moves off-chain. A BLISK spending policy lets each coin move only with the vault and one of the two traders. The venue that matches orders holds no key. Orders clear in sealed 3-second batch auctions that anyone can verify, and each trader holds a signed transaction to exit on Bitcoin.

BlitzPerp is not trustless, and we say so. Our litepaper names the trusted elements, shows what each one can do wrong, and explains the trade-offs.

So I got a Raspberry Pi 3 B+.

Let me walk you through it.

First, it was a bit of a nightmare to install the OS. I don’t know why I struggle with that part and with passwords. I type passwords the way R. L. Stine writes his stories: with just one finger. Either way, I finally managed to install everything and connect to the Wi-Fi.

I knew I would eventually need an electrolytic capacitor and one of those logic level shifters, but for the first trials—just trying to get the Pi and the LEDs working—I left those for later.

I also need a proper power supply for the LEDs themselves. I’m still not entirely sure, since it’s only 32 LEDs, but we’ll see. The preventive side of me will probably end up getting one anyway.

I had to test the first LED strip, but first I had to connect everything to the right GPIO pins and solder the wires. Usually my husband helps me with this part, but he only helped me with the first strip. After that, I was all on my own.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/be570358-1cbc-4a6b-8bc3-ac87d29ad61a_img_8973-213.04.16.gif)

I didn’t know soldering would be as challenging as stripping the wires, but once I got the hang of it, things went much more smoothly.

I did a lot of the research and troubleshooting myself, and for the scripts I also tried a bit of vibe coding. But hey, I was still the one soldering, wiring everything up, testing it, and figuring out what was going wrong. Then I ran the test and… it worked!

But then, of course, came the real challenge... soldering everything together! All the wires and the LED strips.

I had to use the headlamp I use when walking my doggie, and next time I’ll definitely need a magnifying glass. I had to squint from time to time just to make sure I was soldering in the right place.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/55cf9895-d39e-4dc7-9f9f-ad913e468d69_img_9007.jpeg)

I managed to do the devil’s work, I mean, my project, and then I used another script. But before that, I had to install Python in a virtual environment, because otherwise it wouldn’t let me install rpi\_ws281x.

It seems this way is easier to update and keep contained, and it doesn’t affect the rest of the Pi. Also, this time I did everything directly in the terminal. I didn’t use Thonny this time!

So many firsts with this project.

Anyway, in the end, my soldering and the script worked together beautifully!

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/b1a2dfb4-0a23-43af-bf60-3d60bdca4f3d_img_9051.jpeg)

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/24206c44-4240-4671-9556-44dbe83451bd_img_9052.jpeg)

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/e3e233b0-ab4b-4f07-aca9-3ba325358b80_img_9053.jpeg)A sunset right there just for me!

Throughout all this testing, I kept sniffing the Pi and the GPIO area from time to time, just in case I had connected something wrong. After all, powering the LEDs directly from the Pi could be too much for it.

Slowly but surely, I was able to turn the LEDs on and off first. Then I added the sunrise and sunset scripts.

After that, I moved on to the web server. Since I had already dipped my toes into this with [my Raspberrarium](https://stacker.news/items/1541799), I decided this time it wouldn’t just show me information, it would also have buttons to control the LEDs.

Then I added a “reading mode,” a “fun mode,” and a “relax mode.”

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/ea3f6f09-d876-468c-a8ba-16ca6c9813bc_img_9003.jpeg)

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/d82ea84c-1bd2-49b2-99d8-d7cec3dfdd37_img_9017.jpeg)Reading mode

I got super excited watching the first sunset that day. Every five minutes, I would just look at the LEDs slowly dimming.

This week, I added a few more buttons to the web server: some colors, dimming controls, and “demos” of the sunrise and sunset scripts.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/8572001d-7983-45fe-ba49-cedaa6a376a0_img_9054.jpeg)Sunset and Sunrise have buttons though they are running automatically in the background. I still kept them because it reminds me of how this project started. 

What a ride it was!

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/e04c6ebc-0ddc-41f8-885e-c3e097a648a1_freecompress-img_9019.gif)Rainbow mode

And I’m not finished yet. This is still a work in progress, and I’ll add a few more things. I’m so happy with it.

I feel like a wizard.

So, see you later, alligator!

items.title: You Can See Everything - Review
items.text:
## **You Can See Everything**

⚡️⚡️⚡️⚡️ 4/5 Zaps. Worth the sats to see in theaters. One of the best things of the year!

***

https://youtu.be/GGJSRFWALTI?si=7qSyHQI45xohKwnN

I’ll start with what worked, move to what didn’t, and then wrap with the ending and final thoughts.

**TLDR: “You Can See Everything,” is rightly titled because afterward your left wondering what ‘exactly’ did you see.**

***

I don’t think I can rightly review this without **spoiling** everything so starting now consider everything after this with **spoilers**, also should mention you should go into this **unspoiled** if you plan on watching it. I don't think you should watch it any other way. Lastly I have stayed away from every trailer for this movie on purpose, minus this [first teaser.](https://youtu.be/GGJSRFWALTI?si=JYfn_LyZYjCfRSsu)

***

## The Setup

![](https://m.stacker.news/161736)

I don't think this is a documentary in the traditional sense. There's something really interesting about the way the filmmakers carefully control what the viewer gets to see, often presenting events through a collage of tightly framed portrait shots, deliberately staged moments, and sequences that don't necessarily unfold in chronological order.

In fact, I'd be interested in watching this a second time for that reason alone. I suspect knowing what I know now would make it easier to distinguish what's authentic, what's staged, and what's been deliberately manipulated to shape our understanding of the story.

I'm also deliberately calling it a *"thing"* throughout this review because I genuinely don't know what else to call it. It's not exactly a traditional documentary, but it's not entirely a movie either. Much of the second half feels almost entirely like a feature film, with moments that seem so bizarre and unrealistic that you start wondering how much of what you're watching is actually happening the way it's being presented.

And I keep coming back to this point because somewhere around the halfway mark, you realize you're no longer just watching a documentary. You're on a [*"journey"*](https://youtu.be/_8AYmVyIFsc?si=upY9YeUt1HA-2K2E) with Nathan.

But then you begin to realize something else, Nathan isn't necessarily showing you events in the order they happened, nor is he giving you the complete picture. He's carefully deciding what you get to see, when you get to see it, and how you're supposed to interpret it.

That's when I started questioning Nathan himself as a reliable storyteller of what we’re watching because he might be getting tizz whispered by Elizabeth Holmes for most of this.

***

## The Good

![](https://m.stacker.news/161739)

Having said all that, I think what they're doing is brilliant. They're attempting something very few documentary filmmakers have dared to do, openly challenge the idea that you can trust the filmmaker to give you an accurate account of what you're seeing. I know it sounds funny to make this comparison, but there's almost a Christopher Nolan philosophy at work here. Nolan's filmmaking is predicated on trusting the intelligence of his audience, allowing viewers to question what they're seeing and piece things together for themselves.

The filmmakers behind *You Can See Everything* seem to operate from that same philosophy. They don't assume the audience is dumb or incapable of recognizing the sleight of hand happening right in front of them. Instead, they invite you to notice it and purposefully lean into at times that doesn't feel entirely on the nose. I wouldn't call the manipulation necessarily a flaw in the documentary, I think it might actually be the entire point.

The film does this fascinating thing where you think you're watching one story unfold, only to realize Nathan has been showing you exactly what he wants you to see at that particular moment. Then, just when you think you've figured it out, your understanding of what you've been watching completely changes.

I know this might sound like I'm flustered or confused by the whole thing, but I'm really not. Quite the opposite, actually. I think this particular story needed that kind of manipulation of events and perspective to make the whole thing work. And I have to say, this was probably the fastest three hours I've ever spent watching anything.

As for the story itself, it takes you on a wild ride that constantly has you questioning everything you're watching. It starts with Elizabeth Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, but eventually that same skepticism extends to Nathan himself. Nobody is really off limits, including the guy making the documentary.

One of the most interesting surprises, though, is the introduction of [Amanda Seyfried](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1086543/), who, at least for me, ends up stealing the entire movie in what initially seems like a supporting role.

She first enters the documentary to reenact scenes the *You Can See Everything* filmmakers weren't there to capture, including moments from before filming began and later events while Elizabeth Holmes is in prison. But then something really interesting happens. Amanda stops being just an actress recreating events and becomes an actual character in the documentary itself, largely because of Billy Evans' seemingly insatiable need to confront her personally.

Amanda was incredible in [The Dropout](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W7rlZLw9m10), so seeing her show up here genuinely caught me off guard. I'm so glad nobody spoiled that for me. My immediate reaction was basically, [*hmmm, what is she doing here?*](https://plebtv.com/v/the-californians-edit-36cd6601d6) lol.

But what starts as a somewhat bizarre casting decision eventually becomes one of the film's most important elements. Amanda ends up serving as something of a reliable witness within this increasingly unreliable documentary, even calling Nathan out on some of his own bullcrap toward the end.

Just when you've gotten comfortable questioning Elizabeth Holmes, Billy Evans, and their version of events, the documentary turns that same scrutiny back on Nathan.

![](https://m.stacker.news/161737)

Something stackers might enjoy, one interesting thing, is they do bring up cRyPto twitter, and they're is a prominent account that you do see for a split second. You do later find out that Billy her husband is tweeting on her behalf. 🫠

Speaking of money, **greed** is undeniably one of the central themes of this whole thing. You could almost argue that an alternative title for *You Can See Everything* could've simply been *Greed*.

Towards the latter half of the documentary, greed practically steals the show. It becomes this underlying force driving just about everyone involved: A24, Nathan, Elizabeth Holmes, and her husband Billy. Everyone has something to gain, something to protect, or something to lose. And I think that's precisely why this whole thing is so brilliant. It feels entirely intentional, like the YCSE filmmakers are deliberately pulling back the curtain on the very incentives driving the people making and participating in the documentary itself.

And when you combine that greed with the strange dynamics of Elizabeth vs. Amanda and Nathan vs. Billy, the whole thing becomes this bizarre, almost recursive, meta exercise. It's turtles all the way down, except every turtle has its own agenda, its own version of the truth, and its own financial incentives.

***

## The Bad

![](https://m.stacker.news/161738)

There's honestly not a whole lot of bad I can say about this movie, but there are a few things worth mentioning.

For starters, I think watching it with an audience was somewhat enjoyable in the beginning. There's something fun about experiencing a movie this strange with a room full of people who are just as confused or surprised as you are. But as the film went on, some of the things people were laughing at weren't particularly funny to me, and that eventually became a little annoying.

Things also get pretty heated when Amanda starts arguing with Billy, especially when some of her [past comments](https://x.com/DiscussingFilm/status/1998889970942226937) come back into the conversation, particularly those surrounding Charlie Kirk. This is where the theater experience really started to take away from the movie for me. People in the audience began doing that thing where they talk back to the screen, shouting some genuinely awful things that I really wish I hadn't had to sit there and listen to.

And for the record, I saw this movie in Georgia after TabConf, not Texas.

There's also an early nude scene that I thought was pretty dumb and completely unnecessary. It felt like it was thrown in for no other reason than to get a cheap laugh. In a thing that's otherwise so deliberate about what it chooses to show you and why, that moment felt especially out of place.

***

## Final Thoughts

![](https://m.stacker.news/161740)

I'll just end by saying that *You Can See Everything* is genuinely one of the most meta things I've ever watched in my life. It's the kind of film that makes you question not just the story being told, but the very nature of storytelling itself, especially when the people telling the story have their own incentives and agendas.

I genuinely think Nathan and his team might be stumbling onto, or perhaps deliberately inventing, an entirely new genre of documentary filmmaking. It blurs the lines between documentary, performance, manipulation, and reality in a way that feels uniquely suited to his style.

It's rare to watch something that makes you question so much while somehow keeping you entertained the entire time, and leaves you wondering if everything is just a mindgame. Looking forward to see what they create next.

***

items.title: You Walk Your 10k Before Lunch, Anon? (The Economist)
items.text:
**Ah yes, that 10k step goal:** I'm doing ok on the new regime... 9,746 seven-day average!

> Conventional wisdom sets 10,000 steps per day as a good target. The source of that number, though, is as questionable as Hippocrates’s quotation. Its origins lie not in a clinical trial, but a Japanese advertising campaign for a pedometer launched ahead of the 1964 Tokyo Olympics (10,000, in Japanese Kanji, also looks a little like a person walking). Those committed to getting their steps in should not shy away from the 10,000 mark. But in terms of scientific research, the number barely has a leg to stand on.

You *kind of* need a lot of imagination to make this (万) look like a guy walking. [https://www.kanshudo.com/kanji/%E4%B8%87](https://www.kanshudo.com/kanji/%E4%B8%87)

> A study published in *Lancet Public Health* in 2025 considered 57 papers published since 2014 to assess the connection between different daily step counts and various health outcomes. Walking more was found to be beneficial across the board. Taking 7,000 steps a day, in contrast to 2,000, brought about a 47% lower risk of premature death, a 25% lower chance of developing cardiovascular disease and a 14% reduction in the risk of diabetes. Even a little goes a long way: going from 2,000 daily steps to 4,000 resulted in a 36% drop in mortality risk over the years tracked.

wow, *extraordinary!*

## "Extra steps keep helping, but beyond around 7,000 per day, they are scarcely worth the effort. The jump from 7,000 daily steps to 10,000, for example, led to only a 2% further reduction in mortality risk."

> Any reasonable amount of walking is better than none. But for those unable to walk much, upping the pace might be a way to increase the benefits.

...and how neat:

> “And if you don’t have enough opportunities,” says Dr Stamatakis, “create them.” Rather than parking right outside the supermarket, for example, stop around the block and do a walking sprint in.
